Recall once again the relationship among three great mystical Tafsîrs (Qur’anic commentaries; see above, p. 176, note 19). Najm Kobrâ began a Tafsîr but could not finish it. Najm Râzî sought to continue it, while starting again from the beginning of the Qur’an, but got no further than the Sura of the Star. Semnânî then took up the commentary and completed it, adding a prologue and an interpretation of the Fâtiha. Semnânî’s work has a depth and inwardness beyond comparison with that of his predecessors. It is in his commentary on Sura 54 (fol. 12) that Semnânî tells us how Najm Râzî had begun his commentary at the start of the Qur’an and carried it forward. When he reached the Sura of the Star he exclaimed, “How wonderful it would be if God allowed me to undertake the Sura of the Star and bring it to completion!” “But on reaching this sura, he fell ill, and his shining star bore him from the earth of men into the Heaven of divinity.” Semnânî was then inspired to continue and complete the Tafsîr. In it, as in his other writings, he scattered many allusions from which his autobiography can be reconstructed. A short book on his life and works recently appeared in Tehran (Sharh-e ahwâl o afkâr o âthâr-e Shaykh A. S., by Sayyed Mozaffer Sadr). His mystical chain of affiliation (silsila) passes through ’Abdorrahmân Esfarâ’inî ... Najmoddin Kobrâ ... Abû’l-Najîb Sohrawardî, Ahmad Ghazâlî ... and Jonayd Bâghdâdî, back to the Eighth Shia Imam, ’Alî Rezâ (Sadr, op. cit., p. 43). A work by Najm Râzî, Mirsâd al-’Ibâd, is still widely read in Iran today. Chapter XVII deals with visions of coloured lights, the theory of which Semnânî would develop further. ↩

To understand what is involved in the effort to attain anâ’îyat haqqî-ka, the person of your true Self, see the commentary on Sura 114 and what Semnânî suggests in the following anecdote. Jesus was dozing with a brick beneath his head as a pillow. The accursed Devil came and stood beside him. Sensing his presence, Jesus awoke and said, “Why have you come near me, accursed one?” “I have come to collect my belongings.” “What belongings of yours are here?” “That brick on which you are resting your head.” Then Rûh Allah (Spiritus Dei, the Spirit of God—Jesus) seized the brick and hurled it in the Devil’s face. ↩

In his commentary on Sura 112 (fol. 72), Semnânî explicitly discusses the Christian doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation. He knows very well the different ways Jacobites, Melkites, and Nestorians interpreted the relationship between divinity and humanity (lâhût and nâsût) in Christology: how they posed the problem of two natures in a single person or, conversely, affirmed a duality of persons. He knows the name Emmanuel and its meaning (“God with us”), as well as technical expressions such as ittihâd (hypostatic union) and the Son as consubstantialis Patri (ibn jawhar abî-hi, of the same substance as the Father). He offers several interpretations of the three Persons. Yet his understanding of the divine Triad, as generally with our authors, follows a Father–Mother–Son pattern in which the Holy Spirit is conceived as a female hypostasis, or distinct divine reality. This is therefore a conception of the Holy Spirit shared by certain Apocrypha, some Syriac writers (Aphrahat), and Gnosis more generally. We still lack a comprehensive study of the subject, which would cast valuable light on our authors’ sources. Note that this is not simply a grammatical accident arising from the feminine gender of the word “spirit” in Semitic languages. It is truly a conception of a female hypostasis, whose attributes are then transferred to the Angel Gabriel as Holy Spirit and Active Intelligence. Thus Suhrawardî’s Christology, for example, while agreeing with the Qur’an, simply returns to the verse of the Gospel of the Hebrews (“my mother, the Holy Spirit”). See also above, p. 264, note 86. On the Points or Centres mentioned here, see the cosmogony summarized below. As for the idea of an intermediary: just as a child comes into being only through the conjunction of masculine and feminine, so the Centre of Will (noqtat irâdîya) is manifested as proceeding from the active Centre of Knowledge (noqtat ’ilmîya, fâ’ila) and the receptive Centre of Power (noqtat qodrîya, qâbila). These Centres arise from the sea of Jabarût, the higher world of divine power, but the divine Self transcends all Names and Attributes. Only someone who attains the condition of mahbûb (one beloved by God) can glimpse this mystery—someone taken up as Jesus was taken by God into the fourth heaven (4:156), so that the capacity for initiation into the latîfat al-haqqîya may be brought forth within him. ↩

A famous hadith repeated by all the mystics: its words were revealed to the Prophet by the Angel Gabriel, who had heard them from God himself in Heaven ... The human being’s ascent into Heaven (Enoch, Muhammad), birth in Heaven, and theophanic investiture: these movements are the very opposite of a descent that literally incarnates the divinity. Yet the possibility of confusing them was Sufism’s great ordeal, a spiritual temptation. Hence Semnânî’s warning comparison between the Sufi carried away by mystical intoxication and the Christian carried away by dogmatic intoxication. Tafsîr, prologue, fol. 2a. The light of prophecy (nûr al-nobowwat) passes from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to Moses. Each time, the nabîs summon the people of their own cycle toward God through their sharî’at, or revealed religious law. David in turn summons ordinary people through the Torah, while addressing the spiritual elite through his Psalms. So it continues with the nabîs after him, until Jesus is raised up to announce the coming of Ahmad (periklytos, parakletos), the Seal of the Prophets, Lord of the Messengers, and Friend of the Lord of the Worlds. His sharî’at supersedes all other Laws, and the learned men of his community take on a function like that of the prophets in Israel. They summon human beings to his flourishing and conciliatory sharî’at, which makes the straight path easier. Their successors repeat this call century after century until the end of the world, for his religion coincides with the original religious disposition (fitra), just as the structure of the human being is the seal of all births (mawâlîd) in the visible world. On the distinction between ordinary nabîs and the nabîs morsal, or Ulî’l-’azm, whom they succeed—a distinction that becomes very important in analysing the three degrees of latîfat al-haqqîya—see Book I, Chapter VI, and Chapter III, § 9 above. The nabîs play a role in this account of prophecy comparable to the role of the Imams within each prophetic period in Shia prophetology. Notice that the number seven is reached not, as in Ismailism, by the appearance of the cycle’s final Imam as the seventh Nâtiq, but by including David among the Ulî’l-’azm, “with his Book of Psalms addressed to the elite.” ↩

Recall everything we have said in Book I about the relationship between nobowwat (prophecy) and walâyat (spiritual guardianship and initiation). The whole Shia understanding of prophecy is at stake. See also our study Imâmologie et philosophie, in Le Shî’isme imâmite (Strasbourg conference, 6–9 May 1968), Paris, 1970, pp. 143–174. Opposite conclusions about which takes precedence have been drawn from the same proposition: that walâyat is the precondition of nobowwat, and that every nabî (prophet) is first a walî (friend of God). The ’orafâ (mystical gnostics) agree in giving precedence to walâyat, but this precedence may be considered only within the person of the “Seal of the Prophets,” who combines both functions; or it may be regarded as an independent principle, and thus imply the precedence of the Imam. The second position is that of the reformed Iranian Ismailism of Alamût. The resulting “interiorization” of prophetic teachings needs to be studied. On this interiorization in Ismailism, see our Trilogie ismaélienne, index under Imamate, imamology, Olive Tree, and Sinai. Semnânî does not “curse” the first three caliphs recognized by Sunnism, but maintains that each possessed only one aspect of the Imamate, whereas ’Alî ibn Abî-Tâlib possessed all three. Semnânî believes this perfection will be realized again in the Mahdî. He acknowledges that the Mahdî will be a descendant of Fâtima and thus belong to the line of holy Imams. Yet it is far from certain that, in his thinking, this Mahdî is identical with Mohammad al-Qâ’im, son of the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-’Askarî, who is presently hidden in occultation (ghaybat). Thus, although Semnânî’s thought clearly contains a certain Shiism, it is difficult to classify him even as a covert Twelver Shia. The Fatimid Ismaili conception rested on bringing together the three aspects of the Imamate. Furthermore, although Twelver Shia Muslims were not able to establish a state corresponding to their worldview until the Safavid period in the sixteenth century, the Iranian Shia sovereign is not, and cannot be, the Imam in the Fatimid sense. He is the guardian and protector of the community while it awaits the reappearance of the currently Hidden Imam. The idea of ghaybat therefore shapes both individual religious feeling and the form of the state. ↩

The conception of the Imamate in Sunnism, Twelver Shiism, and Ismailism deserves a lengthy comparative study. It has been so neglected that one searches in vain through the articles walî, wasîya, and wilâya in the first edition of the Encyclopaedia of Islam for any reference to the specifically Shia meaning of these technical terms. Without knowing the Shia conception, its premises, and its implications, it is impossible to understand the questions involved here: the Imamate and esoteric interpretation. ↩

On this point, there is a highly important correspondence between Kamâl ’Abdorrazzaq Kâshânî and Semnânî, reproduced by Jâmî in his great Nafahât al-ons (“Breaths of Spiritual Intimacy”). Philosophers carefully distinguish three ontological states. (1) There is what is negatively conditioned (bi-sharti-lâ): the state of a logical concept that excludes every determination that could compromise its emptiness and generality, and therefore its ability to be predicated of everything belonging to a given genus or species. (2) There is what is positively conditioned by a determination (bi-sharti shay’), namely the determination on which its actualization in singularibus, in concrete individuals, depends. (3) There is what is subject to no condition (bi-lâ-shart): neither the negative condition of a concept’s generality nor the positive condition of concrete determination. This is the state of the Avicennian essence, which in itself is indifferent to either condition yet has the potential to be determined by either. It is this third state that is called “absolute” (motlaq, absolutum), “released” from both conditions. Kamâl Kâshânî is distressed that, in criticizing Ibn ’Arabî, Semnânî has apparently confused bi-sharti-lâ with lâ-bi-shart, and he makes considerable efforts to clear up the misunderstanding. But, judging from the position of the later philosophers discussed in our text, we are not convinced that there was a misunderstanding or that Semnânî really confused the two. For those later thinkers, one might say, the word “absolute” (motlaq, absolutum) is a passive participle. It already marks a certain determination and presupposes a pure activity, an absolver (motliq), which releases it from the two possible determinations. Whether this motliq is super-being (hyperousion) or the only being in the true sense, the same shift of perspective occurs. In short, our habits of thought too often make us confuse the empty generality of a concept with the absolutum of the universal—which is the integral, the whole. They also make us pronounce the word “absolute” as though it named a supreme authority, although it silently implies something that makes absolute, an absolvens. We have already treated this question elsewhere (see our study De l’épopée héroïque à l’épopée mystique, Chapter II, “De l’acte créateur comme absolution de l’être,” in Eranos-Jahrbuch XXXV, 1966, pp. 177 ff.). We can therefore see the importance of the correspondence between Kamâl Kâshânî and Semnânî, and its implications for the history of philosophy. It deserves serious study.
